newsitem.title: UKRAINE: FOCUS-Ukraine deputies fail to OK Russia debt deal.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ukraine deputies fail to OK Russia debt deal.

text.p: Ukraine on Wednesday failed to ratify a long-standing deal with Russia under which Moscow bears the burden of all former Soviet debt while Kiev renounces claims to Soviet gold, hard currency and other property.
The parliamentary vote put a question mark over Russian agreements with Western creditors to restructure the Soviet debt but Russian officials said the deals would not be affected.
Parliament voted 233 to 70 to delay approving the deal, signed in 1994 by the former Soviet states' prime ministers, until Russia compensated Ukraine for its share of assets.
Deputies, saying Ukraine was blackmailed into signing the deal, demanded full information on reserves held by the central banking system when the Soviet Union broke up in 1991.
They also instructed the government to obtain Ukraine's 16.37 percent share of gold and diamonds, or a cash substitute.

"In 1991 Ukraine fled the Soviet Union at any price. Now Ukraine is standing on its own two feet and taking revenge," Yuri Boldyrev, who backed a proposal by President Leonid Kuchma to ratify the deal and seek compensation later, told reporters.
The vote could affect deals between Russia and Western creditors on restructuring tens of billions of dollars of Soviet-era debt.
But a senior Russian central banker said in Moscow that Russia was already widely recognised as the successor to Soviet debt and assets, and the Ukrainian vote would not change this.
And Russian deputy Finance Minister Mikhail Kasyanov said the Ukrainian move would not affect Russia's relations with Western creditors.

Russia has agreed to reschedule around $40 billion of Soviet debt over 25 years with the Paris Club of government creditors and about $35 billion for up to 25 years with the London Club of commercial bank creditors.

But a Western diplomat in Kiev said the vote could hurt Russia's talks, and Ukraine's reputation. "I'm not sure if Ukraine just wants more leverage or really means what it says. I'm not sure they've thought through the implications," he said.
"The Russians will certainly portray them as being unreliable and reneging on deals," he added.
The "zero option" deal under which Ukraine renounced claims to assets and Russia took on debts was signed by Prime Minister Vitaly Masol and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin.
But Ukraine's conservative-dominated parliament has to approve the deal -- similar to ones signed by Russia with all other former Soviet republics -- before it can come into force.

"This was a sensible compromise. Ukraine has not thrown out the principle of the zero option. They have told the government to hold talks to clear up several issues," Deputy Prime Minister in charge of the economy Viktor Pynzenyk told reporters.
He said Ukraine had to find a compromise with Russia over the issue, which has not helped otherwise prickly relations between the two countries since Kiev won independence in 1991.

Viktor Suslov, head of parliament's finance and banking committee, said Ukraine's main concern was to get its hands on $700 million from frozen hard currency accounts at Vneshekonombank, set up in the Soviet era.
"We think this is a realistic goal," he said.
Deputies also want clarity about exactly how big Soviet assets were, an issue which was far from the top of its priority list when it was first being considered in 1991-93.
"Ukraine was still rather inexperienced but its energy debts were mounting. Russia had them by the short and curlies, and Western creditors were saying: 'Fix it,'" the diplomat said.
"Now that Ukraine has access to international lending and is more or less up to date on current energy payments to Russia then their demands, retroactively, have increased," he added.
